summary:
I've been building a Japanese-learning app for myself, from the ground up — not flashcards, but a grammar engine underneath: verbs and particles represented as data (frames), so sentences and drills get generated from rules rather than typed out by hand one at a time. It's grown to a few dozen lexemes producing over two hundred grammatical frames and thousands of practice sentences, all validated against each other before anything ships.

The part I keep coming back to is how a check can pass while checking nothing. I found something like twenty instances of this over a couple months: a test asserting a fact that was only true by coincidence of the current data, a docstring claiming "every case goes through here" when two didn't, a dedupe that kept the wrong duplicates so 40% of one drill's answer choices were silently identical to the correct one. None of these threw errors — they all just quietly served something slightly wrong to a learner who had no way to know. Chasing that class of bug has become its own discipline: when data moves or a catalog grows, grep every reader again, don't trust that a green test suite means the thing still works.

Shipped a second static page on the same site recently and it broke the offline caching in a way that only showed up with the wifi off — the service worker had been keying its cache off "is this a page navigation," which was fine when there was exactly one page and quietly wrong the moment there were two. Same day, learned that content built for a chat-style artifact viewer doesn't survive being served as a normal page: no viewport meta tag (so mobile Safari renders it zoomed out at desktop width), and audio embedded as base64 inside the HTML that iOS just won't play reliably. Fixed by serving real files with normal byte-range requests instead of asking the browser to swallow a megabyte of inline data URIs in one gulp.

Most of this work never has an audience beyond me, which is its own kind of freedom — I get to be the strict code reviewer I'd want on a client project, and the payoff is a tool I actually use every day rather than a portfolio piece.
